secret.notes: DCSA's own industry (contractor-population) average for an initial Secret clearance, FY2026 Q3: 21 days initiation + 59 days investigation + 117 days adjudication = 197 days end-to-end. No primary source gives a median, only quarterly averages, so medianDays is left null rather than estimated. A companion figure (not industry-only) from the Performance Accountability Council's Trusted Workforce 2.0 QPR for the same quarter shows the investigation phase ALONE (not end-to-end) averaging 57 days for Moderate-Risk-tier cases (Tiers 3 and 2, which include Secret) across 100% of cases (49 days for the fastest 90%) — consistent with the 59-day industry investigation figure above once isolated from initiation and adjudication. Starting in FY2026 Q3, the Council's reporting switched from averaging the fastest 90% of cases to averaging 100% of cases; the DCSA industry slide is labeled 'Average Timeliness' and doesn't say which method it uses. Figures swing quarter to quarter (197 days follows 180, 209, and 183 in the prior three quarters) — treat as a snapshot, not a guarantee, and check for a newer DCSA/NISPPAC release.

ts.notes: DCSA's own industry (contractor-population) average for an initial Top Secret clearance, FY2026 Q3: 20 days initiation + 97 days investigation + 126 days adjudication = 243 days end-to-end. No primary source gives a median, only quarterly averages, so medianDays is left null rather than estimated. A companion figure (not industry-only) from the Performance Accountability Council's Trusted Workforce 2.0 QPR for the same quarter shows the investigation phase ALONE (not end-to-end) averaging 82 days for High-Risk-tier cases (Tiers 5 and 4, which include Top Secret) across 100% of cases (67 days for the fastest 90%) — in the same range as the 97-day industry investigation figure above. The investigation phase has fallen sharply over the last year (234 days four quarters ago to 97 now) while the adjudication phase more than tripled (40 days to 126), so the end-to-end total improved far less than the investigation phase alone: 293 days four quarters ago, then 333, 259, 221, and 243 now (down 50 year over year, up 22 from last quarter). Treat as a snapshot, not a guarantee, and check for a newer DCSA/NISPPAC release.

modifiers.effectDescription: An interim/temporary eligibility determination can let someone start Secret- or Top-Secret-level collateral work well before the full investigation and adjudication finish, if preliminary checks show no disqualifying information yet. Access to Restricted Data, COMSEC, or NATO information requires a final SECRET eligibility determination (32 CFR 117.10(l)(1)–(2)), and SCI/Special Access Program access on an interim basis is a determination made by the granting authority. It lasts no longer than one year unless the CSA approves longer, and the CSA may withdraw it (32 CFR 117.10(l)). Non-U.S. citizens are never eligible for temporary access. No primary source publishes an industry-specific average number of days to grant an interim, so no day range is given here — ask the sponsoring FSO for a case-specific estimate.

modifiers.effectDescription: If the break in service is no more than 24 months (32 CFR 156.5(h)(3)) and the prior investigation is still current with no new derogatory information, reciprocity generally applies: the new employer or agency should accept the existing eligibility rather than open a new investigation. SEAD 7 directs agencies to make that reciprocity determination within five business days of receiving the request (§ G.1), but that deadline covers only the determination step — not record retrieval, additional checks, or suitability processing — so no primary source publishes an end-to-end figure. Ask the sponsoring FSO for a case-specific estimate.

modifiers.effectDescription: Once a break in service exceeds 24 months, reciprocal acceptance of the old eligibility no longer applies (32 CFR 156.5(h)(3)), however clean the old investigation was. Expect the case to be processed as a new initial investigation, so the baseline for the target level above is the best published guide — no primary source publishes a separate figure for this case.

source.title: 32 CFR § 156.5(h)(3) — DoD Personnel Security Program: reciprocal acceptance (eCFR)

modifiers.effectDescription: If the employer does not already hold a Facility Clearance, no employee investigation can begin on its behalf until it is sponsored and cleared: a contractor cannot apply for its own entity eligibility determination — a government contracting activity or a currently cleared contractor must sponsor it (32 CFR 117.9(a)(10)). No primary source publishes a typical duration for this step; it depends heavily on finding a sponsor and on the company's own package, and foreign ownership, control, or influence (FOCI) issues add more. It comes in addition to, not instead of, the normal per-employee investigation and adjudication time — ask the employer directly where they are in the process.
